# Abstract

Thailand experienced one of the most dramatic demographic and spatial transformations in post-war Asia, expanding from 17,1M inhabitants in 1945 across 547.158 km² of national territory to 71,6M by 2025. Following the termination of the Second World War, the kingdom initiated public health initiatives, including widespread DDT house-spraying campaigns against endemic malaria, rural sanitation drives and antibiotic distribution. These interventions cut crude death rates from over 28 per thousand in the late 1940s to below 9 per thousand by the mid-1970s. As infant and child mortality collapsed while total fertility rates remained above six births per woman, natural increase accelerated to 3,2% annually during the late 1950s and 1960s, doubling the national population in less than twenty-three years and driving extensive pioneer colonisation of forested uplands across the Khorat Plateau, the upper central river valleys and the northern intermontane basins.

This explosive growth was followed by an exceptionally swift fertility transition coordinated by the National Family Planning Programme, inaugurated in 1970. Leveraging village health volunteers, mobile clinical vans and non-governmental social marketing initiatives, the total fertility rate plummeted from 6,13 births per woman in 1965 to replacement level (2,1) by 1990, declining further to 1,16 by 2024. Consequently, national demographic expansion shifted from high-pressure natural increase to rapid population ageing, workforce stabilisation and structural labour shortages. Concurrently, spatial settlement patterns underwent intense geographic concentration, creating an extreme monocentric urban hierarchy anchored by Bangkok. The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration expanded into a vast urbanised region encompassing Nonthaburi, Samut Prakan, Pathum Thani, Samut Sakhon and Nakhon Pathom, while manufacturing agglomerations coalesced along the Eastern Economic Corridor in Chonburi and Rayong.

MANDALA reconstructs this post-1945 demographic arc through the systematic harmonisation of nine decennial and quinquennial national censuses conducted by the National Statistical Office between 1947 and 2020, reconciled with annual civil registration records and 4.183 georeferenced settlement trajectories. By partitioning the kingdom into six physiographic and economic macro-regions, the analysis resolves administrative boundary splits, compensates for differential municipal under-enumeration, and disaggregates unregistered internal circular migration between agrarian provinces and industrial districts. The resulting spatial matrix establishes an enduring baseline for historical demography across Mainland Southeast Asia, demonstrating how agrarian frontier closure, state-sponsored reproductive healthcare and globalised industrialisation reshaped settlement distribution across eight decades.

# Background

## Post-War Recovery and Epidemiological Transition

In the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, Thailand retained an agrarian demographic regime governed by high fertility and volatile infectious mortality [@V2011Health; @Waxler1982Fertility]. While the kingdom had avoided direct colonial administration, wartime Japanese military occupation, severe shortages of imported pharmaceuticals and Allied bombing had disrupted internal transport networks and public health facilities [@V2011Health]. Malaria remained the preeminent killer across the humid foothill zones and forested frontiers of the North, the Northeast and the Bilauktaung ranges, claiming tens of thousands of lives annually and suppressing agricultural settlement in uncleared valleys [@Mahikul2019Modelling].

Beginning in 1949, the Ministry of Public Health, supported by the World Health Organization and the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund, launched nationwide residual insecticide spraying campaigns using DDT [@V2011Health]. Within a single decade, malaria mortality fell by over 80%, transforming formerly lethal forest fringes into arable pioneer frontiers. Concurrently, systematic vaccination campaigns against smallpox, tuberculosis and cholera, alongside maternal and child health clinics established in district sanitary districts (*sukhaphiban*), caused infant mortality to decline from over 105 per thousand live births in 1947 to 48 per thousand by 1970 [@V2011Health; @Waxler1982Fertility]. This rapid epidemiological transition occurred prior to broad industrialisation, creating a widening demographic gap between falling mortality and sustained high fertility that generated unprecedented population pressure throughout rural Thailand, modifying marriage patterns and household reproduction [@Goldstein1978Migration].

## Agrarian Pioneer Frontiers and Upland Colonisation

Between 1950 and 1980, rural Thai households responded to rapid demographic increase not by mass urban migration, but through horizontal agricultural expansion [@Goldstein1978Migration; @Guest1998Assessing]. Thailand possessed an extensive land frontier composed of dry dipterocarp forests, alluvial terraces and undulating plateaux that had remained sparsely populated during the absolute monarchy. As household sizes expanded, younger generations migrated into uncleared public domain lands, clearing millions of hectares for sedentary cultivation [@Guest1998Assessing; @Mahikul2019Modelling].

This frontier expansion exhibited distinct regional trajectories:
1. The Khorat Plateau of Northeastern Thailand (Isan): Smallholders cleared vast tracts of scrub woodland along the Mun and Chi river basins, establishing rainfed paddy fields alongside commercial upland crops such as cassava, kenaf and maize. The Northeast absorbed millions of new settlers, cementing its position as the demographic reservoir of the kingdom [@Mahikul2019Modelling; @Phelawan2025Experiment].
2. The Upper Central Plains: In Kamphaeng Phet, Sukhothai, Phichit and Nakhon Sawan, opening of the Phahonyothin Highway and the construction of the Chao Phraya dam irrigation complex in Chai Nat facilitated double-cropping of rice and extensive sugarcane farming [@Tsuda2023Macroscopi].
3. The Northern Intermontane Valleys: Migrants moved up the river terraces of Chiang Rai, Phayao and Nan, establishing irrigated paddy systems in intramontane basins while hill-dwelling ethnic minorities expanded upland swidden systems.
4. The Southern Maritime Littoral: Rubber smallholdings and commercial oil palm plantations expanded across forested hills in Surat Thani, Krabi, Trang and Songkhla, attracting southern cultivators and migrant labour from the central and northeastern provinces into perennial export agriculture and coastal enterprises [@Pongponrat2015Domestic; @Witvorapong2015Social].

By the late 1970s, the agrarian frontier encountered severe physical limits. Forest cover contracted from 53,3% of national land area in 1961 to under 28% by 1988, prompting the royal government to institute a nationwide commercial logging ban in January 1989. With the closure of the terrestrial frontier, rural demographic absorption ceased, redirecting surplus rural labour toward urban and industrial labour markets [@Guest1998Assessing; @Shummadtayar2013Investigat].

## The National Family Planning Programme and Fertility Collapse

Faced with population growth rates exceeding 3% annually that threatened to overwhelm national education budgets, healthcare infrastructure and agrarian resources, the Thai government promulgated an official National Population Policy in March 1970 [@Waxler1982Fertility]. The policy aimed to lower natural increase through voluntary family planning, integrated directly into basic maternal and child healthcare services across rural health centres.

The Thai fertility transition achieved singular velocity due to several institutional factors [@Waxler1982Fertility; @Goldstein1978Migration]:
- Decentralised paramedical delivery: Auxiliary midwives and nurse-practitioners were legally authorised to prescribe oral contraceptive pills and insert intrauterine devices, bringing reproductive services directly to sub-district (*tambon*) clinics.
- Community-based distribution: Innovative non-governmental social marketing organisations, popularised by Mechai Viravaidya and the Population and Community Development Association, destigmatised contraceptive use through humour, village competitions and accessible community distribution networks.
- High female economic autonomy: Thai women historically enjoyed high rates of agricultural and commercial labour force participation, inheritance rights under matrilineal kinship structures and geographic mobility, fostering rapid receptivity to smaller family norms [@Goldstein1978Migration; @Tschirhart2020Choosing].

The demographic response was swift. The total fertility rate collapsed from 6,13 in 1965 to 4,9 in 1975, 3,42 in 1980, 2,17 in 1990 and 1,53 in 2000 [@Waxler1982Fertility; @V2011Health]. By 2020, total fertility fell below 1,25 births per woman, and by 2024 it reached 1,16, among the lowest figures globally. Thailand completed its demographic transition in thirty years, experiencing dramatic population ageing before attaining high-income economic status [@Hattapradit2026Ageing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial].

## Bangkok Urban Primacy and the Eastern Seaboard

The spatial counterpart to Thailand's demographic transformation was the intensification of extreme urban primacy [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin]. Throughout the twentieth century, Bangkok operated as the solitary metropolitan focus of Thai political administration, higher education, finance and international commerce [@Sawetthapong2023Factor; @Sawetthapong2023Using]. In 1947, Bangkok and its twin city Thonburi housed approximately 780k inhabitants, roughly six times the population of the second largest settlement, Chiang Mai. By 1980, the conurbation accommodated over 4,6M people, and by 2020 the contiguous urban agglomeration housed over 10,5M residents within the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration and adjacent perimeter provinces [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Songsom2025Examining].

Beginning in the late 1970s, the Thai government initiated the Eastern Seaboard Development Programme along the eastern Gulf coast in Chonburi and Rayong [@Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin]. Anchored by deep-sea commercial ports at Laem Chabang and Map Ta Phut, petroleum refineries and automotive manufacturing clusters, the Eastern Economic Corridor attracted massive domestic and foreign capital investment. This corridor emerged as a secondary industrial agglomeration, absorbing hundreds of thousands of migrant workers from the agrarian provinces of Isan and the Central Plains while remaining integrated into the metropolitan supply chains of Greater Bangkok [@Guest1998Assessing; @Pongponrat2015Domestic].

## Internal Circular Migration and Remittance Economies

A defining structural mechanism of post-1970 Thai demography was the institutionalisation of seasonal circular migration [@Guest1998Assessing; @Goldstein1978Migration]. Because rainfed agriculture across the Khorat Plateau is strictly limited by the southwest monsoon calendar (May to October), millions of Northeastern smallholders experienced protracted dry-season underemployment. Following the harvest of wet-season rice in November, working-age adults moved en masse to Bangkok, the Central Plains and the Eastern Seaboard to take up temporary employment in construction, taxi driving, textile manufacturing and food processing [@Guest1998Assessing; @Pongponrat2015Domestic].

These cyclical population flows generated vital remittance corridors that sustained rural living standards. Financial transfers sent back to rural villages funded agricultural machinery, fertiliser inputs, house reconstruction using corrugated zinc and concrete, and schooling fees for children who remained in the care of grandparents [@Guest1998Assessing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial]. This skipped-generation household structure became a standard feature of Northeastern rural sociology, with direct impacts on elderly dependency and rural living standards [@Hattapradit2026Ageing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial]. When economic shocks struck urban centres, such as the 1997 Asian financial crisis, hundreds of thousands of retrenched factory labourers returned temporarily to their natal villages, demonstrating that the rural agrarian sector operated as a vital demographic shock absorber for the national economy [@Guest1998Assessing; @Mahikul2019Modelling].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Territorial Boundaries

To analyse demographic trajectories across eight decades without administrative distortion, MANDALA adopts a rigid spatial grid framework [@Tsuda2023Macroscopi; @Thanvisitthpon2018Urban]. The terrestrial territory of Thailand (547.158 km²) is partitioned into 6.751 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km). Each cell is assigned to one of six historical-geographic macro-regions:
1. Bangkok Metropolitan Region and Lower Central Plains: 70.843 km², encompassing the capital conurbation, the lower Chao Phraya and Tha Chin river basins, and coastal provinces along the inner Gulf.
2. Upper Central Plains: 91.876 km², spanning the alluvial rice plains of Nakhon Sawan, Phitsanulok, Kamphaeng Phet and surrounding foothill districts.
3. Northern Thailand: 100.159 km², comprising the intermontane valleys and forested highlands of Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Lampang and Mae Hong Son.
4. Northeastern Thailand (Isan): 174.740 km², covering the expansive sandstone undulating plains of the Khorat Basin and Sakhon Nakhon Basin bounded by the Mekong River.
5. Eastern Economic Corridor: 33.855 km², encompassing the maritime industrial littoral of Chonburi, Rayong, Chachoengsao and the forested interior of Prachin Buri and Sa Kaeo.
6. Southern Thailand: 75.685 km², covering the Isthmus of Kra, the Bilauktaung and Phuket ranges, and the maritime border provinces along the Gulf of Thailand and Andaman Sea.

Sub-provincial administrative reorganisations, including the creation of new provinces (*changwat*) such as Yasothon (1972), Phayao (1977), Mukdahan (1982), Sa Kaeo (1993), Nong Bua Lamphu (1993), Amnat Charoen (1993) and Bueng Kan (2011), are harmonised backward across all decennial benchmarks to maintain strict geographic consistency [@Tsuda2023Macroscopi].

## Census Harmonisation and Civil Registration Correction

Thailand's modern census sequence comprises nine complete decennial and mid-decade national enumerations: 1947, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, supplemented by official population balance estimates for 1945 and 2025 [@Goldstein1978Migration; @Guest1998Assessing]. Harmonising these counts requires addressing two primary structural discrepancies:
- Differential under-enumeration: Post-enumeration surveys conducted by the National Statistical Office reveal net census undercounts ranging from 1,8% in rural agrarian districts to over 7,5% in the Bangkok Metropolitan Area, where high-density tenement housing and transient workforces elude municipal census canvassers [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Pongpiachan2025Size].
- Civil registration divergence: The Department of Provincial Administration maintains a continuous household registry (*thabian ban*). Because internal migrants often retain their registered domicile in their natal rural villages to preserve agricultural land claims and local health entitlements, civil registration systematically under-records Bangkok's de facto residents while over-recording de facto populations in rural Isan and the North [@Guest1998Assessing; @Pongponrat2015Domestic].

MANDALA adjusts these raw counts through dasymetric reconciliation, calibrating de facto census returns against satellite-derived night-time luminosity, residential building footprints and land-use rasters to distribute transient worker populations to their authentic physical locations [@Songsom2025Examining; @Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To prevent demographic double counting between nucleated urban settlements and dispersed rural cultivators, 4.183 catalogued settlements with longitudinal population series are anchored to precise WGS84 coordinates. Settlement positions are cross-referenced with national gazetteers and Thailand Fine Arts Department GIS (FADGIS) inventories. At each benchmark year, the summed urban population of catalogued settlements within each sub-region is subtracted from the sub-regional total:

$$P_{\text{rural}}(t) = P_{\text{total}}(t) - \sum_{i=1}^{K} P_{\text{settlement}, i}(t)$$

The residual rural population is then dasymetrically distributed across non-settled terrestrial pixels in proportion to multi-layer environmental suitability weights, incorporating slope, proximity to perennial rivers and irrigation canals, road density and agricultural land suitability, while taking account of seasonal inundation patterns [@Thanvisitthpon2018Urban; @Tsuda2023Macroscopi].

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the six macro-regions, their territorial extents, benchmark demographic trajectories and 2025 population densities.

# Testing and Validation

## Remote Sensing Cross-Check and Urban Footprint Mapping

Settlement spatial bounds and population densities were cross-examined against multi-temporal satellite remote sensing archives, including historical Corona reconnaissance photography from the 1960s, Landsat MSS/TM series from 1972 onward, and high-resolution Sentinel-2 and night-time luminosity records [@Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin; @Songsom2025Examining]. In the Bangkok Metropolitan Region, satellite imagery documents the transition from canal-based ribbon settlements (*khlong*) to arterial road corridors following the construction of the Superhighway (Vibhavadi Rangsit), Sukhumvit Road and the Outer Ring Road networks [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Pongpiachan2025Size].

These remote sensing surveys confirm that urbanised land cover expanded at more than three times the rate of population growth between 1980 and 2020, as lower-density industrial estates, golf courses and suburban residential estates (*muban chat san*) engulfed formerly agricultural paddy landscapes across Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan [@Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin]. Satellite-derived impervious surface rasters corroborate the demographic decentralisation of central Bangkok toward peri-urban industrial belts and atmospheric emission zones [@Saeyang2026Principal; @Songsom2025Examining].

## Demographic Transition Cross-Validation

The trajectory of Thai fertility decline was corroborated against international demographic surveys, notably the 1975 Survey of Fertility in Thailand (conducted under the World Fertility Survey), the Contraceptive Prevalence Surveys of 1978, 1981, 1984 and 1987, and the Demographic and Health Survey series [@Waxler1982Fertility; @Goldstein1978Migration]. These micro-level surveys demonstrate extraordinary consistency with decennial census age cohorts, confirming that age-specific fertility rates dropped across all educational and income strata simultaneously [@Waxler1982Fertility; @V2011Health].

The alignment between registered vital statistics and backward-projected cohort-component models indicates an average census completion rate exceeding 97,5% nationally, establishing Thailand's post-1960 demographic data as among the most reliable in Southeast Asia [@Goldstein1978Migration; @V2011Health]. In addition, contemporary spatial indices of population ageing and elder dependency confirm the long-term momentum generated by this transition across both rural provinces and metropolitan districts [@Hattapradit2026Ageing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA settlement gazetteer for Thailand was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion methodology designed to eliminate spatial omissions and toponymic homonyms:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official census publications from the National Statistical Office and municipal registers from the Department of Provincial Administration, capturing 2.593 primary administrative settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of urban and peri-urban localities from institutional geographic catalogues, municipal development plans and gazetteers, incorporating 1.129 secondary centres.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill of foundation chronologies, municipal status upgrades (*thetsaban nakhon*, *thetsaban mueang*, *thetsaban tambon*) and sanitary district transitions, adding 461 historical settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps across all six macro-regions cross-checked against administrative gazetteers and Thailand Fine Arts Department GIS (FADGIS) inventories, confirming zero unaccounted settlements and achieving asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 4.189 candidate records were audited: 4.183 were accepted as unique settlements and 6 were excluded due to duplicate spatial buffering within a 2,2 km deduplication radius.

# Results

## National Demographic Trajectory and Growth Epochs

Thailand's demographic trajectory from 1945 to 2026 reveals four distinct phases: post-war population boom, agrarian frontier expansion, rapid fertility transition and twenty-first-century demographic stabilisation and ageing (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Macro-Regional Chronological Analysis

### Post-War Reconstruction and High Natural Increase (1945 to 1960)

Between 1945 and 1960, Thailand's population expanded from 17,1M to 26,26M, adding 9,16M people in fifteen years at an average annual growth rate of 2,9%. In 1945, Northeastern Thailand was already the most populous division with 5,13M inhabitants (30% of the kingdom), followed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Region and Lower Central Plains with 4,79M (28%), Southern Thailand with 2,39M (14%), Northern Thailand with 2,05M (12%), and the Upper Central Plains and Eastern division with 1,37M each (8% each).

During this period, DDT spraying and mass immunisation drastically reduced mortality across the rural provinces. The 1960 census, the first conducted with modern United Nations technical assistance, recorded 26,26M inhabitants, demonstrating that population growth had outpaced pre-war projections. The Northeast expanded to 7,88M, while Greater Bangkok grew to 7,35M, initiating high-density settlement infill throughout the central delta [@V2011Health; @Goldstein1978Migration].

### The Agrarian Frontier Boom (1960 to 1980)

The two decades from 1960 to 1980 represented the climactic phase of terrestrial settlement expansion. National population surged from 26,26M in 1960 to 34,4M in 1970 and 44,83M by 1980, adding 18,57M inhabitants in twenty years at an average annual growth rate of 2,71%. In the Northeast, population climbed to 10,32M in 1970 and 13,45M in 1980, as smallholder families cleared upland forests for commercial crops [@Mahikul2019Modelling; @Phelawan2025Experiment].

Concurrently, the Bangkok Metropolitan Region and Lower Central Plains expanded to 9,63M in 1970 and 12,55M in 1980. Industrial estates developed along the Phahonyothin and Bang Na-Trat corridors, attracting rural youth seeking wage employment. Southern Thailand grew from 3,68M in 1960 to 6,28M in 1980, supported by the boom in natural rubber and tin extraction, while Northern Thailand expanded from 3,15M to 5,38M [@Goldstein1978Migration; @Pongponrat2015Domestic].

### Industrial Reorientation and Fertility Collapse (1980 to 2000)

Between 1980 and 2000, national population increased from 44,83M to 60,92M. While absolute numbers expanded by 16,09M, the annual growth rate declined sharply from 2,31% in the early 1980s to 1,05% by the late 1990s as the reproductive impact of the National Family Planning Programme took hold [@Waxler1982Fertility].

With the closure of the terrestrial frontier and the 1989 logging ban, the nature of Thai migration changed fundamentally. Rural-to-rural frontier colonisation ceased, replaced by large-scale circular migration from the agrarian Northeast and Upper Central Plains toward the Bangkok conurbation and the newly established Eastern Seaboard industrial estates [@Guest1998Assessing]. In the Eastern Economic Corridor, population climbed from 3,59M in 1980 to 4,87M in 2000, while Greater Bangkok surged to 17,06M, generating contiguous suburban settlement across adjacent provinces [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Songsom2025Examining].

### Megalopolitan Primacy and Demographic Ageing (2000 to 2026)

In the twenty-first century, Thai demographic growth approached an asymptote. Population grew from 60,92M in 2000 to 65,98M in 2010, 70M in 2020 and 71,6M by 2025. Between 2010 and 2025, annual growth slowed to 0,54%, with projections indicating a definitive population peak around 2029 followed by natural contraction [@Hattapradit2026Ageing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial].

The spatial landscape is characterised by deep demographic divergences. While the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (20,05M in 2025) and the Eastern Economic Corridor (5,73M in 2025) continue to attract internal migrants and over 3M cross-border migrant workers from Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, rural provinces in Northern Thailand (8,59M) and the Upper Central Plains (5,73M) have entered absolute demographic decline due to ultra-low fertility and youth out-migration [@Suksai2020Foreign; @Tschirhart2020Choosing]. Northeastern Thailand, with 21,48M inhabitants in 2025 (30% of national population), remains the primary demographic reservoir, but its rural villages are increasingly populated by ageing cohorts sustaining skipped-generation households [@Hattapradit2026Ageing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial].

The settlement structure of Thailand exhibits extreme urban primacy:
1. Primate Megalopolis: Bangkok commands the urban hierarchy with an official registered population exceeding 5,68M in 2020 and a peak recorded population of 8,28M, expanding to over 14M when including the contiguous suburban and industrial districts of Samut Prakan (1,35M peak), Samut Sakhon (1,35M peak), Nonthaburi (1,33M peak) and Pathum Thani (1,33M peak) [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Sawetthapong2023Factor].
2. Major Provincial Capitals and Regional Hubs: Secondary centres include Surin (1,33M peak), Roi Et (1,31M peak), Chiang Rai (1,29M peak), Si Sa Ket (1,29M peak), Songkhla (1,26M peak), Sakon Nakhon (1,15M peak), Chaiyaphum (1,14M peak), Nakhon Ratchasima (1,09M peak), Nakhon Sawan (1,09M peak) and Surat Thani (1,06M peak).
3. Industrial Corridor Municipalities: Along the Eastern Seaboard, conurbations such as Chonburi, Si Racha, Pattaya and Rayong form a high-density industrial corridor housing hundreds of thousands of manufacturing workers [@Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin; @Songsom2025Examining].

# Limitations

Demographic reconstruction across post-1945 Thailand encounters specific methodological and archival constraints:
1. Registration-Residence Divergence: The divergence between civil registration (*thabian ban*) and de facto census enumeration introduces persistent uncertainty in sub-provincial allocations. Hundreds of thousands of temporary and seasonal migrant workers residing in Bangkok dormitories, construction sites and fishing ports retain rural registration in Isan, distorting per-capita infrastructure and municipal density metrics [@Guest1998Assessing; @Pongponrat2015Domestic].
2. Cross-Border Undocumented Migration: Thailand hosts an estimated 3M to 4M cross-border migrant workers from Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, concentrated in fisheries, domestic service, agriculture and construction. Because documentation status fluctuates with periodic government regularisation amnesties, decennial censuses undercount these populations in maritime provinces such as Samut Sakhon, Ranong and Tak [@Suksai2020Foreign; @Tschirhart2020Choosing].
3. Boundary Reclassifications: The progressive upgrading of sanitary districts (*sukhaphiban*) to sub-district municipalities (*thetsaban tambon*) following the 1999 Municipality Act abruptly reclassified millions of rural residents as urban without physical relocation, complicating longitudinal urbanisation rate calculations [@Shummadtayar2013Investigat; @Iamtrakul2024Quantifyin].
4. Upland Minorities and Environmental Exposure: In the upland border zones of Northern Thailand, statelessness and delayed citizenship registration among ethnic minority populations led to under-enumeration in mid-twentieth-century censuses, while coastal settlements in Southern Thailand face acute environmental hazards such as tsunami and coastal flooding risks [@Witvorapong2015Social; @Tsuda2023Macroscopi].
5. Urban Mental Health and Social Vulnerability: In the high-density metropolitan agglomeration of Bangkok, accelerated urban growth has intensified psychosocial stressors among secondary and tertiary students alongside interpersonal vulnerabilities across congested residential quarters [@Pisitwanichakul2023Correlation; @Seeya2024Structural].

# Conclusion

Between 1945 and 2026, Thailand traversed the full trajectory of modern demographic modernisation, expanding from 17,1M post-war inhabitants across 547.158 km² to 71,6M by 2025. This expansion was propelled initially by post-war public health initiatives that suppressed mortality, triggering thirty years of rapid growth and widespread agrarian frontier colonisation across the Khorat Plateau, the northern valleys and the southern littoral [@V2011Health; @Waxler1982Fertility].

The subsequent introduction of the National Family Planning Programme in 1970 facilitated one of the swiftest fertility transitions recorded in demographic history, lowering total fertility rates from over 6 births per woman to below replacement level within three decades, and ultimately to 1,16 by 2024 [@Waxler1982Fertility; @Goldstein1978Migration]. Consequently, Thailand faces profound population ageing, labour contraction and regional demographic divergence, contrasting an expansive megalopolitan core in Greater Bangkok and the Eastern Economic Corridor with depopulating rural hinterlands [@Hattapradit2026Ageing; @Tontisirin2024Spatial]. MANDALA reconciles these dynamic processes through harmonised spatial and census frameworks, establishing an enduring baseline for Southeast Asian historical demography.
